Q: Is there any way to implement HTTP/3 (QUIC) in Apache HTTP Server? A:

No there is no way at present. Apache has not committed to doing the work required here at this time.

LiteSpeed is an Apache alternative supporting many of the same features, but with strong QUIC and HTTP/3 support.

Nginx also has only made vague comments about QUIC and HTTP/3 but Cloudflare have made an Nginx patch available that adds QUIC and HTTP/3 support. (Edit Nginx have since previewed HTTP/3 support built independently of Cloudflare’s implementation).

Or alternatively Caddy is another alternative server with QUIC and HTTP/3 support.

However, if I were looking to enable, or even just experiment, with QUIC and HTTP/3 I would look to a CDN as they will be the simplest way to enable this and ensure you have optimal settings. Cloudflare has a free plan that (I think) also includes HTTP/3 and QUIC support so is easy to set up in front of a site you own.

Q: laravel 8 module form error The POST method is not supported for this route. Supported methods: GET, HEAD A:

Try to use action="/create" in your form like so:

<form class="form-horizontal" action="/create" enctype="multipart/form-data" method="post">

I don't work with PHP and have no prior experience with Laravel but I can see that you are creating a route for the POST /create endpoint. With your current form object you reference the route action with a relative URL. So, if the form is on a page under the /path/to/form route, then the form submission results in a call to the POST /path/to/create route instead of the (maybe) intended POST /create route.

Q: Why does `Object.groupBy()` return an object where `hasOwnProperty` is not a function? A:

Object.groupBy() intentionally returns a null-prototype object.

This means the returned object does not inherit from Object.prototype, so methods like hasOwnProperty, toString, etc. are not available.

const grouped = Object.groupBy(people, p => p.role);

Object.getPrototypeOf(grouped) === null; // true

Why is it designed this way?

The main reason is to avoid prototype collisions.

If the result inherited from Object.prototype, a group key could overwrite built-in properties:

Object.groupBy(data, x => "toString")

With a normal object, this could conflict with Object.prototype.toString.

By returning a null-prototype object, the result behaves like a pure dictionary where all keys are safe and there are no inherited properties.

How to check properties

Since hasOwnProperty is not available, use:

Object.hasOwn(grouped, "dev");

or

Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(grouped, "dev");

This behavior is intentional and follows the same design pattern used by objects created with:

Object.create(null)


const people = [
  { name: "Ana", role: "dev" },
  { name: "Ben", role: "dev" },
  { name: "Cara", role: "pm" }
];

const grouped = Object.groupBy(people, p => p.role);

console.log("Grouped result:", grouped);

console.log("Prototype:", Object.getPrototypeOf(grouped));

console.log("typeof hasOwnProperty:", typeof grouped.hasOwnProperty);

console.log("Check property with Object.hasOwn:", Object.hasOwn(grouped, "dev"));

Q: python function argument set reuse, with variations in internal code A:

This sounds like an XY Problem, and the most Pythonic thing to do here is almost-certainly what's most clear to others!

You're probably best served by another solution like

  • creating a function with an additional argument to choose which logic path it follows (similar to what you propose)
  • creating two normal functions and using them normally
  • creating a class which keeps all or most of the arguments as properties, and which then both functions are modified to expect an instance of as an argument
  • creating a class and making both functions methods of the class (easily shares logic via methods)

That said, if you do choose to have two complete functions, it probably does make sense to add a unit test ensuring their arguments are ordered exactly the same to avoid later confusion!

Finally, and while it's a bit of a hack, when calling the function, you can supply **locals(), unpacking all the local names as arguments to a function and allowing you to avoid naming them all during the call!.. however I would only do this for special cases where more terse or dynamic code really is more clear and helpful to readers

Q: Is there a way to stream ollama chat into a Marimo ui? A:

mess is a list with objects ChatMessage() and you have to convert it to dictionary.

messages=[{"role": item.role, "content": item.content} for item in mess],

Or you can use only last item if you don't want history

messages=[{"role": "user", "content": mess[-1].content}],

Full working code

from ollama import chat

model = "llama3.2"


def simple_stream(messages, config):

    stream = chat(
        messages=[{"role": item.role, "content": item.content} for item in messages],
        model=model,
        stream=True,
    )

    for chunk in stream:
        yield chunk["message"]["content"]


mo.ui.chat(simple_stream, prompts=[""])

Q: Building a Custom Read-Only iSCSI Target on Windows (Physical Disk Export) A:

Is user-mode implementation (Winsock + raw disk reads) sufficient, or is a kernel-mode StorPort/virtual SCSI driver required?

user-mode is sufficient. the target is simply a network server parsing TCP packets.

Which Windows components or tools are needed (Windows SDK, WDK)?

only need Windows SDK(C/C++).

If implemented as read-only at SCSI level, is it architecturally safe from disk corruption?

It is architecturally safe if implemented correctly.

the core engineering workload is writing the protocol parser: stripping away the TCP/iSCSI PDU (Protocol Data Unit) encapsulation to extract the raw SCSI Command Descriptor Blocks (CDBs).

Once you extract the SCSI CDB, your Windows application acts as a pure SCSI emulator—translating commands like READ (10) into Win32 ReadFile() calls, and strictly rejecting WRITE commands.

Q: Interop.Excel not working with Office 2024 A:

If you’re using Microsoft.Office.Interop.Excel with Office 2024 and it’s not working, this is often due to version or COM registration issues. Office 2024 may introduce changes in COM IDs or require updated Primary Interop Assemblies (PIAs).

Steps to resolve:

  1. Check references: Make sure your project references the correct version of Microsoft.Office.Interop.Excel compatible with Office 2024.

  2. Install PIAs: Ensure the Office 2024 PIAs are installed. Sometimes you need to install them via the Office installer under “Add or Remove Features → .NET Programmability Support.”

  3. Use Embed Interop Types = True: In your project references, set Embed Interop Types to True to avoid version conflicts.

  4. Verify COM registration: Open regedit and check that the Excel COM server is correctly registered under HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\Excel.Application.

  5. Consider alternative APIs: If Interop is unreliable, Microsoft recommends using Open XML SDK or Microsoft Graph APIs for Office automation in modern versions.

Example:

using Excel = Microsoft.Office.Interop.Excel;

var excelApp = new Excel.Application();
excelApp.Visible = true;

If this throws exceptions, it’s usually a missing PIA or COM registration issue.

Q: Shift key and Copilot key A:

The Copilot policy doesn’t change key mappings. You’ve remapped the scancodes.

  1. Open regedit, go to
    HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Keyboard Layout.​

  2. Delete Scancode Map if it exists, reboot.​

Or use PowerToys → Keyboard Manager and remove any remap involving Left Shift/Copilot key.
